rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to ensure all 10 compounds elute within the 42 min acquisition window while revealing the overall elution window and any critical pairs. All compounds eluted well within the gradient, so the next step is to trim the gradient window to the actual elution region to gain time while keeping a similar slope. This should keep all peaks in-gradient and test whether a focused window improves the already only moderately critical cluster around peaks 5–7.

The narrow low-organic window over-retained the last compound, so return to the broad window and now vary only gradient time to probe slope sensitivity. A shorter gradient should improve the time term substantially and reveal whether the closest cluster around peaks 5–7 is robust or slope-limited.

Comparing 10 vs 20 min shows the critical 5–7 cluster is strongly slope-sensitive, so test an intermediate gradient time to recover resolution there while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve a near-zero time penalty. This directly targets the current tradeoff between CRF terms.

The 6/7 pair improves markedly as the gradient is made shallower, and 14 min is already near-optimal with no time penalty, so the next step is a small move to 16 min to see if resolution can be pushed to baseline without yet incurring meaningful time cost. This exploits the clear slope dependence while staying close to the current best method.

The main remaining lever is selectivity: at 16 min all pairs are resolved but time penalty appears, while 14 min is faster yet just misses for the 6/7 pair. Keep the near-optimal 14 min slope and shift temperature to test whether a modest selectivity change can separate that critical pair enough to reach full resolution with zero time penalty.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by creating a new 5/6 overlap, so test the opposite direction at the best fast gradient. If the close cluster reorders favorably at higher temperature, we may achieve full resolution while retaining the zero time penalty seen at 14 min.

Temperature clearly changes selectivity within the central cluster, and at 35 C the problematic contact shifted from 6/7 to 5/6. Combining that selectivity shift with a slightly steeper gradient may open 5/6 while accepting some compression elsewhere, mapping whether there is a better local tradeoff than the 14 min, 40 C condition.

The data indicate slope is the dominant handle and temperature moves only which pair is limiting. Since 16 min fully resolves the mixture but incurs only a small time penalty, 18 min tests whether the scoring optimum might sit just beyond 16 if the CRF time penalty grows slowly while preserving full resolution.

At 14 min the last peak still elutes well before the gradient end, so the broad 0.05–0.95 window is likely steeper than necessary.
